blocks.text: Explicit Rules for Changing an Order

We now define the operations in this model. Only an order in preparado may change its unit count, be shipped, or be canceled. Changing the count requires another quantity between one and twenty. Shipping changes the state to enviado, and canceling changes it to cancelado. A shipped or canceled order can no longer be changed through these operations. The code and quantity are preserved when the order is shipped or canceled.

Each operation returns bool: true if it applied the requested change, and false if it rejected the request without modifying any member. Here, a disallowed request is a normal outcome under the contract. Invalid construction still throws an exception: we do not replace it with a fallback order.

blocks.question: Why do we not assign nuevas first and then check whether it belonged to the allowed domain?
options: Because nuevas already has type int and its values do not need validation.
Because returning false automatically undoes any previous assignment.
Because a rejected request could leave the value temporarily or permanently invalid, requiring a rollback.
blocks.explanation: Checking first provides a straightforward guarantee that rejection makes no changes.

blocks.text: The class does not carry out every request regardless of its order. A table containing the previous state, request, result, and subsequent state makes the decisions visible without attributing them merely to the operation's name.

Having between one and twenty units is part of the invariant. Being in preparado is a condition for changing the unit count, shipping, or canceling; it is not required of every existing order because an order in enviado is also valid. An operation may be rejected even while the object remains perfectly valid.

blocks.question: A shipped order with four units…
options: Is valid under the invariant, but this interface no longer allows changing its unit count.
Is invalid because it is no longer in preparado.
Allows changing its unit count whenever the new quantity is valid.
blocks.explanation: Distinguish the validity of an object's state from whether an operation is available.

blocks.question: After shipping, a rejected cambiar_unidades(5) request must leave…
options: The same code and enviado state, but the requested five units.
The same code and quantity, but the preparado state.
The same code, quantity, and state that the object had before the request.
blocks.explanation: The rejection contract requires every member to remain unchanged.

Implement the Pedido model with the three operations described. Construct {"Q", 4}; change the quantity to six; ship the order; try to change it to seven; and try to cancel it. Display the results of those four requests as 1 1 0 0 and the final quantity as six. Also test canceling before shipping, shipping twice, and changing quantities at each boundary and neighboring values.

Write a state table for the variations. The criterion is not merely to end with a number within the range: rejections must also preserve the code and state, and every transition must require preparado.

Criteria: each transition is applied only from preparado; changing units checks the quantity before assignment; false preserves every member; true performs exactly the documented change; the constructor still rejects invalid initial data. Use the const queries to observe the object after every request.

blocks.question: Which test distinguishes this guarantee from an implementation that returns false but still changes the unit count?
options: Repeat an accepted request without inspecting the object.
Compare the members before and after a rejected request.
Look only at the returned bool.
blocks.explanation: The reported result and actual side effects must satisfy the same contract.
